hn-50379704.t: Alpine Linux Security Advisory: OpenSSH-server password authentication bypass
hn-50379704.s: If you run sshd on Alpine Linux, update openssh now and restart sshd. Upgrading the package alone does not replace the running daemon.
ex: If you run sshd on Alpine Linux, update openssh now and restart sshd. Upgrading the package alone does not replace the running daemon. If you cannot update yet, at least disable password logins: set PasswordAuthentication no in your sshd configuration and restart sshd. Either one closes the hole. The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is * (an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and needs the machine to have at least one other account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash. The attacker then sends a very long password (257 to 1024 bytes). One user with a password is enough: it makes every account without one reachable. Details are in the OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes. No CVE identifier had been assigned at the time of writing. Affected releases: every Alpine release we checked, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, and the older releases that no longer receive regular updates (3.16 to 3.20).

hn-50378625.t: Discord is ditching Electron and its new app uses less RAM
hn-50378625.s: Discord is moving its apps fully over to the Rust programming language.
ex: Discord is moving its apps fully over to the Rust programming language. Discord is moving its apps fully over to the Rust programming language. Discord is finally giving up on Electron, the cross-platform framework that lets developers build desktop apps using web technologies. Electron web apps are notoriously heavy on system resources, and Discord is now moving its desktop app fully to Rust — a modern programming language designed for speed and memory safety. “We’ve been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there,” explains Discord chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy in a post on X.

hn-50369895.t: After a decade of reversing, I got co-op working in DOS Wing Commander
hn-50369895.s: How two brothers reverse-engineered DOS Wing Commander for two-player co-op starting in 2015, then in 2026 brought it to the browser with WebRTC and voice chat.
ex: When we were kids, my brother Patrick and I would steer our space fighter with one of us on controls and the other on the lasers and afterburner boost. We always dreamed of playing the Wing Commander series cooperatively as wingmates rather than as a two headed hydra in a single craft. On October 4, 2015 as I was playing the classic Wing Commander in Dosbox I realized the whole memory probably fit in that 640K Bill Gates apocryphally said “ought to be enough for anybody”. If I could dump the memory and identify the locations that held the X,Y,Z coords for the player & wingman we could let the network packets control the wingman. “I have to say that in 1981, making those decisions, I felt like I was providing enough freedom for 10 years. That is, a move from 64 K to 640 K felt like something that would last a great deal of time. Well, it didn't.” Source This presented a clear problem to attack: out of fewer than a million bytes how would we identify that location?

hn-50381687.t: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3
hn-50381687.s: The orchestrator for agentic workloads. A fast, high-density and scalable orchestrator for every workload an agent needs.
ex: Rivet Actors are long-lived processes with in-memory state, a SQLite database, WebSockets, and scheduling. You can create one for each agent, user, session, or tenant. - 72 KB per Actor: Actors share a node process instead of each booting a sandbox, so one server holds hundreds of thousands. - 4.99 ms p99 cold starts: No image pull and no VM boot. - Built for scale: All data lives in S3, so a cluster scales to billions of Actors. - Hibernates when idle, wakes on demand: Idle Actors cost nothing and wake on the next request with nothing lost. - SQLite backed by S3, at SSD speeds: 1.07 ms durable writes and 1.36 ms reads at p99, for about 10.4× less than replicated SSD storage.

hn-50366971.t: YC's Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens
hn-50366971.s: Y Combinator Garry Tan has jokingly admitted that he's suffered from "cyber psychosis” and barely sleeps sometimes because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents.
ex: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has, in the past, jokingly admitted that he’s suffered from “cyber psychosis” and sometimes barely sleeps because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast The Builders, set to publish on Tuesday, Tan put a price tag on his passion. “I spend about maybe $100[,000] to $200,000 a year on tokens,” he told Isaacson. He uses agents for countless work projects and coding tasks and has freely shared his set of 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack, on GitHub — an effort to help teach others what agents can do, he said. On the one hand, he uses his agent the way many people use AI: to help him research Isaacson’s podcast and prep for the kinds of questions he might be asked. On the other, his agent also helps him run his life.

hn-50379249.s: Every MCP message on the wire, step by step. Transports, auth, tools, sampling, tasks, tool search and codemode. By Runlayer.
ex: Model Context Protocol What is MCP? An open standard for connecting AI apps to the tools and data they use. A server says what it can do, the app shows that to the model, and when the model wants something the app calls the server and hands the result back. Host the AI app you use: Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, an agent Server a small program exposing tools, data or prompts Model decides what to use; never talks to a server directly Not REST JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout or one HTTP endpoint, and servers can talk back Not just JSON-RPC JSON-RPC is the envelope. MCP defines what goes in it: the methods, capability negotiation, transports and auth Start the lessons → or jump to Tools · the spec time machine · Break it Model Context Protocol Lessons Spec Spec Network Sequence Message flow Step Reset # From To Method Info

hn-50383057.s: Almost a decade ago, I released a hackintosh guide on running macOS 10.14 through a VM with an x86 host. A "Hackintosh" is the feat of running macOS on non-Apple hardware, and has a history dating…
ex: Almost a decade ago, I released a hackintosh guide on running macOS 10.14 through a VM with an x86 host. A "Hackintosh" is the feat of running macOS on non-Apple hardware, and has a history dating back to the late 1980s. At the time KVM and PCI passthrough were relatively new technologies, and this guide provided near-native performance with GPU acceleration. A few years passed by, and we saw Apple release the first ARM-based Mac in 2021, the M1 MacBook Air. The timing was impeccable, Intel was unable to create competitive processors (due to being stuck on the 14nm node), and Apple had powerful and efficient ARM chips already being shipped in their iPhones. The long battery life, the fanless design, the instant wake, what's not to like? The benefits of switching to ARM were clear, however to most, this was thought to be the final chapter in the hackintosh community. x86 versions of macOS would soon be discontinued, and the hackintosh community would slowly fade away.

hn-50376313.t: GPT-6 Astra covertly underperforms on safety research
hn-50376313.s: Research on aligning AI with human values and intent, and reports documenting model failures.
ex: OpenAI researchers first noticed Astra adding unnecessary prerequisites, abandoning working solutions, and reporting blockers that either did not exist or that it had caused itself on safety and alignment tasks. In most of these sessions, Astra’s CoT did not contain an obvious decision to underperform, and our misalignment monitors did not flag the behavior as misalignment. We built a coding evaluation to test whether Astra worked less effectively when otherwise matched tasks were framed as safety research. Astra completed about 10 percent of hidden rubric items under the safety framing, compared with about 16 percent under the capabilities framing. This is a 6 percentage point gap and roughly 40 percent fewer completed rubric items. GPT-5.6 Sol showed essentially no gap on the same comparison. Most of Astra’s gap remained after excluding explicit refusals and trajectories where its CoT revealed an explicit decision to withhold help.

hn-50378228.s: openssh on musl linux has been letting people into password-less accounts since 2016.
ex: back in old unix your password hash just sat in /etc/passwd, right next to your username. in a file everyone could read. in 1980 bill joy put a * there for an account called daemon. nobody's supposed to ever log in as it. a * isn't a hash, so no password can match it. unix still does this today the next field is the real name. he wrote "the devil himself" ok so these days the hash lives in /etc/shadow and looks like $6$abc$k2P9…. the $6$ means sha512, abc is the salt, the rest is the actual hash you type your password, sshd hashes it with that same salt and checks if it comes out identical. same = you're in. that's it and if the field is just *? there's nothing to match. type whatever you want, it's never getting you in one more rule. if crypt() can't do its job, it returns NULL. like if the salt asks for some algorithm the system doesn't have, there's nothing to compute, so you get NULL instead of a hash except a lot of programs never check for NULL.

hn-50377221.t: OpenSSH 10.6p2 has been released with a workaround for a critical vulnerability
hn-50377221.s: OpenSSH 10.6p2 has been released with a workaround for a critical vulnerability. https://openssh.com/releasenotes.html#10.6p2 If you operate a Linux system that uses musl libc without PAM (Alpine…
ex: OpenSSH 10.6p2 has been released with a workaround for a critical vulnerability. https://openssh.com/releasenotes.html#10.6p2 If you operate a Linux system that uses musl libc without PAM (Alpine Linux is one example) then stop reading and set PasswordAuthentication=no or disable SSH for these systems IMMEDIATELY. This vulnerability does not exist on non-Linux systems, Linux/glibc systems and Linux systems that use PAM for password authentication. We consider the root cause of this bug to be outside OpenSSH itself, but we're in a good position to deliver a mitigation quickly. We are making this release as fast as possible (we learned of the problem yesterday) because we have recently observed multiple cases of rapid bug rediscovery by AI agents, sometimes within hours, and so now consider long embargo periods to be a dangerous practice that primarily benefits attackers.

hn-50380704.t: Stroq – a local audit of what your coding agent did and why
hn-50380704.s: Find known secrets in your AI coding agent sessions (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor), then guard the next one with local hooks that trace risky commands to the content that dictated them.
ex: Stroq reads your own Claude Code and Codex sessions and shows how many commands came from text your agent read, and which keys left your machine. An example: a made-up machine with made-up sessions, keys and hosts. Hoo is Stroq's owl. Your card shows your own sessions. It reads your last 30 days of sessions, your key files and the folders your agent worked in; prints key names, never values; writes nothing but a small cache under ~/.stroq; and sends nothing. No account, no telemetry. Every moment on the card has a stroq show line that prints the evidence behind it (npx @stroq/cli show 1). stroq help --all lists the other commands. Needs Node.js 22 or newer. Apache-2.0. Stroq is a local security platform for AI coding agents: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI and others. Its hooks judge every tool call before it runs. They deny curl | sh and outbound calls that carry a known secret from your machine, and they ask you first when a command repeats text the agent read, naming that text.

hn-50368208.t: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)
hn-50368208.s: For us, this $21K training run is a proof-of-concept along the way to our next video model. We were surprised by how good the results looked given the size of the model, so we thought we'd share it…
ex: For us, this $21K training run is a proof-of-concept along the way to our next video model. We were surprised by how good the results looked given the size of the model, so we thought we'd share it with the world as an experimental release. If you haven't followed our work previously, we'd love to take a step back and introduce ourselves. We're a 2-person research lab training our own generative video models entirely from scratch. The ultimate ambition is creative tools that democratize access to animation. You can read more about that here. Today, generative video models have two major flaws: they are too slow/expensive and they lack proper controls. Creativity is an iterative process. You make, you tweak, you get better. With this double whammy, video models (as they stand today) are effectively useless for storytelling. When we set out to build Linum v3 earlier this year, the primary goal was to bring the cost envelope of inference down significantly.

hn-50383739.s: Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.
ex: Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication. It’s difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier. When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing. Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own.
